# Education in Nigeria
Education in Nigeria begins with six years of primary education, typically starting around age five, culminating in a first school-leaving certificate. The Universal Basic Education (UBE) program, established in 1999, ensures nine years of free and compulsory schooling covering primary and junior secondary levels. Subjects include Mathematics, English, religious knowledge, agricultural science, and indigenous languages. Secondary education follows a "9-3-4" system, with three years each of junior and senior secondary schooling. Senior secondary students take a curriculum of core and elective subjects, concluding with the Senior Secondary Certificate Examination (SSCE) administered by the West African Examination Council (WAEC) and the National Examination Council (NECO). Admission to federal secondary schools is merit-based via national entrance exams; state schools face varying funding and teacher qualification challenges, while private schools often have better resources and qualified staff.
Tertiary education comprises federal, state, and private universities, polytechnics, monotechnics, and colleges of education with over 150 universities registered. Entry typically requires satisfactory SSCE results and passing the Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) examination. Vocational education is coordinated by the National Board for Technical Education and the National Business and Technical Examinations Board, offering technical certificates and apprenticeships, though funding and implementation remain inconsistent. Notably, informal education and literacy programs play a significant role but face funding and policy challenges. Female education initiatives target increased enrollment and retention, addressing barriers such as poverty and cultural factors. Despite progress, literacy rates remain uneven, with ongoing government efforts emphasizing digital literacy and universal access. Nigeria hosts numerous international schools offering foreign curricula, and advanced level programs like IJMB and JUPEB enable university direct entry bypassing standard admission processes.
